Listen to this article Share Earlier this month, voters in the US state of Iowa elected Rob Sand, a Democrat, as governor. As state auditor, Sand had brought two people, a Republican and an independent, who had donated to his opponent into his senior team. He wanted people close enough to see a mistake coming and independent enough to tell him while there was still time to change his mind. Advertisement Advertisement In Nigeria, we have a phrase for the opposite instinct: “Oga knows best.” It can pass for a joke or a courtesy. The trouble begins when it becomes a rule of professional survival. In a ministry, a boardroom or a newsroom, people learn to read the person in charge as carefully as they read the evidence. A proposal can go from tentative to inevitable without anyone critically examining it, simply because everyone has worked out whose proposal it is. Those who could have spotted its defects have learnt the wisdom of keeping quiet. A proposal can go from tentative to inevitable without anyone critically examining it, simply because everyone has worked out whose proposal it is. Those who could have spotted its defects have learnt the wisdom of keeping quiet. By the time those defects become public, it is too late, the costly consequence of Groupthink. The psychologist, Irving Janis, used the term to describe how the pursuit of agreement, at all costs, crowds out much needed critical appraisal. The genuine dissenter is not necessarily an assigned “devil’s advocate”, who has been called to argue a case they may not believe. The dissenters arrived at a different judgement, by themselves, and are willing to say so. Experiments by the psychologist Charlan Nemeth suggest that genuine dissent can prompt a wider search for alternatives than an assigned objection. The dissenter can be wrong and still improve the discussion, because the objection may expose an assumption that no one else had thought to question. The hardest person to hear is often not the frenzy mob in the street shouting, ‘Bamaiyi! It is the colleague inside it who knows the work and has no wish to see it fail. Too often, there is no adult voice in the room, bold enough to clearly articulate the mob’s position and why, to the Oga-Patapata. Abraham Lincoln brought rivals such as William Seward and Salmon Chase into his Cabinet. But not every leader will have Lincoln’s confidence. Dissent can be institutionalised, a notion advocated by Peter Drucker and Warren Bennis. A dissenting opinion on the US Supreme Court puts on record an argument the majority did not accept. Toyota’s Andon system gives a worker the means to flag a defect and stop the production line. The two have different purposes and stakes, but both give an objection somewhere to go, without waiting for an invitation from the Oga-at-the-Top. Christopher Kolade told a story from his days at Cadbury that brings the point closer to home. The board had decided that distributors should pay before receiving goods. A sales manager in Aba explained that the policy would not work in the market he knew; it ran against the way traders there did business. Advertisement The board reconsidered. Its members had the authority to decide; the manager had knowledge they needed. What makes the episode noteworthy is that the manager spoke up, and the people who could have ended the conversation by invoking the board’s authority let his knowledge count against their own settled decision. President Umaru Musa Yar’Adua made room for opposition figures in his government of national unity and was willing to hear critics. At The Guardian, publisher Alex Ibru gave his editors latitude rather than treating ownership as a license to dictate opinions. These are examples of what some leaders made possible; they did not necessarily institutionalise dissent. What happens when a generous proprietor is succeeded by an intrusive one? The dissenter arrived at a different judgement, by themselves, and are willing to say so. The difference between a leader who listens and an institution that can hear is clearest when an objection is unwelcome. Does an official’s warning reach the minister before a costly public commitment is made? Does a director’s objection survive in the minutes when management would rather move on? Can a reporter question a line favoured by the proprietor and still be trusted with the next story? In each case, the danger is that loyalty to the institution’s work will be read as disloyalty to the person who runs it. The point here is not to give the dissenter veto power. Critics can be vain, badly informed or wrong, and there comes a point when somebody must decide. A minister may have good reasons to proceed despite a warning, just as a board may reject a director’s objection. But there is a difference between a warning that has been weighed and one that never reached the table. And a record of why a decision was taken gives an institution something to learn from if events prove it wrong. Advertisement Advertisement The hardest person to hear is often not the frenzy mob in the street shouting, ‘Bamaiyi! They can be dismissed as partisan and political. The hardest person to hear is the colleague inside who knows the work and has no wish to see it fail. Too often, there is no adult voice in the room, bold enough to clearly articulate the mob’s position and why to the Oga-Patapata. That is the voice Rob Sand did not want missing or silent at his inner circle table. That was what the sales manager in Aba brought to the Cadbury boardroom: knowledge the people above him did not have. He did not need to take their place. He needed them to hear him. A country can be rich in talent and still squander it by teaching people that the surest path to promotion is to withhold the judgement for which they were hired.
